Limanowa Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Limanowa, Poland

Not demolished. Limanowa, first mentioned in 1476 and chartered in 1565, saw Jewish settlement from the early 17th century (written records from 1640); an independent community, initially subordinate to nearby Wiśnicz's kehilla, likely formed in the second half of the 19th century, growing from 100 residents (13%) in 1841 to 571 (36%) by 1890. A brutal WWI battle here in 1914 killed roughly 42,000 Russian and Austrian soldiers combined. By 1939, over 1,000 Jews lived in Limanowa; a wartime ghetto held about 2,000 Jews from the region, and over 500 people were murdered across multiple execution sites in and around town, including this cemetery - the largest single event being a 1941 shooting of 167 Jews at Stara Wieś. The ghetto was liquidated July 17, 1942, sending survivors to the Sowliny labor camp, a second Stara Wieś execution (about 200 killed), or the Nowy Sącz ghetto en route to Bełżec. This cemetery, likely established in the mid-19th century, had its tombstones used for street paving and stone benches; restoration memorials followed in the 1970s and 1990s (initiated by Leib Gatterer and Henryk Rosenbaum), with a separate symbolic matzevah later erected at the Stara Wieś mass-grave site by the Zapomniane Foundation.
